messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was forty-three days into captivity when he stopped counting. The warehouse in rural Pennsylvania had become his entire world—a concrete box with two small, high windows that let in only the grey light of late autumn. His captors, a group of men he'd angered in a financial dispute that had spiraled into something darker, kept him isolated. They fed him irregularly, sometimes withholding food as punishment. What haunted him most, though, wasn't the physical confinement but the psychological warfare: they would play recordings of children crying through a speaker in the corner of the room, sometimes for hours. They said it was to "teach him empathy," to break him down. They made him do things—write letters, confess to crimes he hadn't committed, perform humiliating acts in front of them—all while reminding him that no one knew where he was, that no one was coming. When rescue finally came, seventy-two days later, Marcus emerged from that warehouse a man fractured at his foundation.

Three years have passed since his release, and Marcus, now thirty-seven, sits in his apartment in Philadelphia with the blinds drawn. He works remotely as a financial analyst—a choice he made to avoid the commute, the open office, the exposure. The captivity left him with a conviction that feels as real as his own heartbeat: he had violated something essential about himself. He had compromised his values to survive, had become complicit in his own degradation. That sense of violation resurfaces whenever his ex-wife's new partner tries to embrace him at custody handoffs, or when he hears his ten-year-old daughter cry over a scraped knee. The physical affection that once felt natural now triggers a cascade of shame and revulsion—not at the person offering it, but at himself, at what he had become in that warehouse. And the children crying, always the children crying. His daughter's tears are innocent, but they transport him instantly to that speaker, to the recordings, and in that moment he is certain he deserves this punishment, that he is fundamentally corrupted.

The night terrors began within weeks of his release. Marcus found he couldn't fall asleep without first checking every door, every window, without positioning his bed so he faced the entrance to his bedroom. His hypervigilance at home has become so ingrained that he now sleeps only three or four hours a night—not from insomnia, but from the constant vigilance he maintains. He lies awake, alert, scanning for threats that his rational mind knows aren't there but his nervous system refuses to dismiss. This alertness feeds his memories. In the darkness, waiting for sleep that won't come, his mind becomes a cinema for the past. The smell of the warehouse—diesel fuel, concrete dust, human waste—surfaces unbidden. When he does sleep, his dreams are indistinguishable from reality; he wakes gasping, convinced he is still there. These vivid, visceral memories are far more real to him than ordinary recollections. He cannot conjure the face of his college roommate, but he can see with perfect clarity the rust stain on the metal chair where they made him sit.

The memories are inseparable from his conviction of his own dehumanization. As he lies awake, replaying moments of compliance and shame, he confronts the evidence of his own objectification: he had been treated as a thing to be used, broken, and ultimately discarded. That he survived by cooperating with his captors, by performing the degradations demanded of him, only deepens his sense that he is no longer fully human. This belief crystallizes whenever he encounters reminders of the men who held him. None have been prosecuted. Two are still alive, living ordinary lives, while Marcus remains imprisoned by the memory of what they made him do. The absence of accountability—the fact that they have faced no consequences—reinforces his conviction that the world recognizes what he now knows about himself: that he is diminished, that his violation was deserved, that he is an object among objects.

His daughter's upcoming birthday party terrifies him. There will be noise, children, the possibility of sudden silence followed by a child's scream. His ex-wife has asked him to attend. He has already begun planning his absence, rehearsing excuses. He came to therapy because his therapist at the clinic suggested it, not because Marcus believes anything can truly change. What he fears most is that someone will touch him with kindness and he will recoil, confirming what he already knows: that he is broken beyond repair.
